sources.title: How much running is too much? Identifying high-risk running sessions in a 5200-person cohort study
sources.authors: Schuster Brandt Frandsen J, Hulme A, Parner ET, Moller M, Lindman I, Abrahamson J, et al., Nielsen RO
sources.population_design_dose: 5205 adult runners (mean 45.8 y, 22% female), Garmin GPS data, 588,071 sessions, 18-month follow-up; exposure = single-session distance relative to the longest run in the previous 30 days.
sources.findings: Single-session spikes >10-30%, >30-100% and >100% above the 30-day longest run were associated with higher overuse-injury rates (HRR 1.64, 1.52, 2.28); week-to-week ratio showed no association and ACWR an inverse one.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (exposure definition); Results Table 1; Discussion, Limitations.
limitations: Observational; authors state a preventive 10% rule needs randomized evidence.
Distance, not duration; self-reported injury; binned, non-monotonic hazard ratios.
counterevidence: Weekly progression metrics were not associated with injury in the same cohort.

literature_snapshot.counterevidence_search: Counterevidence was sought by re-running my unchanged kit and R7ASC probes on the frozen runtime with predecessor controls, by reproducing the author's kit run, and by new bounded probes (a 99-return walk/jog matrix, the walk/jog-to-continuous boundary on two athletes, progression authority on two runners, a RETURN-mode control, an R6-H25 trace), each run on this freeze, on STATE-MODEL-CONSUMER-FREEZE-1 and on STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1.

claims.statement: On this freeze a return whose pause begins in the walk/jog exit week, before any continuous run, resumes continuous running at the exit dose (SHORT) or as RETURN/RESTART continuous runs (MODERATE, LONG) while the last session run was the step-8 walk/jog session.
claims.applicability: Walk/jog athletes completing the ladder (zero, unknown or low running exposure at intake).
limitations: Synthetic timelines only; no real athlete, product data, human or empirical validation.
counterevidence: A pause beginning inside the last ladder week, or after one continuous run, returns correctly.

claims.statement: The approved recipe says a SHORT return resumes the last executed doses and the next step waits for executed sessions, a MODERATE return steps conditionally to the prior executed dose, and this contract's W2 says a step the evidence released but the athlete never ran is not tolerated yet; the exit is the ladder's next step after step 8.
claims.applicability: Policy conformance (R6-SSCTR-NONCLINICAL-RETURN r12 conditions; R7ADA-CONTRACT-1 C').
limitations: A governance reading of approved rules, not new evidence.
counterevidence: The single-run ceiling (operational.run.singleRunCeiling) explicitly bounds WALK_JOG->EASY transitions and return steps at the 30-day longest run plus one step, and 25 = 20 + 5 meets it; it is a ceiling, not an exception to the return recipe.

claims.statement: A first-week-back prescription of three 25-minute continuous runs when the longest run in the preceding 30 days is the 20-minute step-8 jog is a single-session increase of about 25% over the 30-day longest run, the band (>10-30%) a 5,200-runner cohort associated with higher overuse-injury rates (R6-S02); the policy itself only allows such a step response-gated and disclosed, which a return after a break is not.
claims.applicability: Recreational adult runners; applied here to runners just off the walk/jog ladder.
limitations: Observational, distance-based cohort of experienced recreational runners, not novices; association, not causation.
counterevidence: Weekly progression metrics showed no association with injury in the same cohort.

claims.statement: Whether the MODERATE path's frequency increase (continuous runs on five days where the athlete ran three) harms novices is not established by any source I hold.
claims.applicability: MODERATE returns of walk/jog athletes at the exit.
limitations: Single-session durations stay at or below the longest continuous run executed (15 and 20 min against 20).
counterevidence: R6-S02 found no association for week-to-week ratios.

records.applicability: Walk/jog athletes whose pause begins in the exit week before their first continuous run; SHORT carries the material part, MODERATE and LONG the recipe part.

decision.rationale: F4 is closed inside the ladder (my 12-cell probe 0/12, predecessor 10/12; my 99-return matrix 0/99, predecessor 29/99, STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 4/99; the essential case 'step A tolerated, step B only projected' closed). At the ladder's last transition it is not: W2 caps the walk/jog step only while the state's mode is WALK_JOG, so a released but never-run exit (mode EASY) passes through and the return treats continuous running as already tolerated. Pre-existing (identical on the predecessor and on STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1), not introduced by this freeze, and inside the F4 scope the Founder set (§20 matrix 'transition to continuous running'; brief item 12).
preserve: W1 and W2 for every ladder step, the projected-only boundary fix and P7 (a continuous run executed makes the exit the return base).
The walk/jog SHORT, MODERATE and LONG recipes and the single-run ceiling.
modify: Recommendation R46 (not implemented here): extend W2 to the ladder exit. When the run state left WALK_JOG through walkJogExit and no continuous run of that state has been executed (P7), the state a return reads is the walk/jog state at the step of the last walk/jog session executed; SHORT then resumes step 8, MODERATE step 7 and LONG step 0. Re-run ssctr-r7ada-continuous-probe.mjs (expect ladderView 0 in every EXIT_EARNED cell, ONE_CONTINUOUS_RUN and the cross-week cells unchanged), the walk/jog matrix (0/99), my 12-cell walk/jog probe (0/12) and the kit grids.
decision.mec_change_level: One condition in the state a return reads (historicalRun in stateAtBreak); no new policy, no state-model change.
decision.trade_off: A walk/jog athlete pausing in the exit week repeats the last ladder step for one executed week before the exit, the cost of the approved 'next step waits for executed sessions'.
must_not: Must not return a walk/jog athlete above the step last run, the exit included, unless a continuous run of the exit was executed.
Must not withdraw walk/jog from V1 or weaken W1/W2 to close this.
conditions: Scope: offline synthetic Node24 reference only, for the adult (18+) recreational nonclinical V1 population stated in PROGRAM_POLICY_R6.population. Missing current eligibility is ASK; pain, injury, illness, functional limitation or a clinical interruption reason is CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED with no substitute dose.

sources.authors: Nuuttila OP, Nummela A, Korhonen E, Hakkinen K, Kyrolainen H
sources.population_design_dose: 30 recreational runners, matched-pair randomized, 15 wk; predefined program (2 progressive weeks with +10% volume then a -25% recovery week) versus load adjusted twice weekly from HRV, perceived recovery and HR-speed index.
sources.findings: Both groups improved; individualized group improved 10-km time more (-6.2% versus -2.9%) with fewer low responders; HIT block used 6x3 min at maximal sustainable effort.
limitations: Small sample; HRV-dependent monitoring; negligible strength training.
counterevidence: Predefined progression was also effective.

sources.title: Effects of Short- and Long-Term Detraining on Maximal Oxygen Uptake in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Zheng J, Pan T, Jiang Y, Shen Y
sources.population_design_dose: 21 studies of trained individuals after training cessation.
sources.findings: VO2max decreased after short-term (ES -0.62) and more after long-term cessation (ES -1.42).
limitations: VO2max only; heterogeneous definitions of short/long; athletes.
counterevidence: No difference between 30-90 and >90 days in subgroup analysis.

literature_snapshot.counterevidence_search: Counterevidence was sought by re-running my unchanged kit and R7ASC probes on the frozen runtime with predecessor controls, by reproducing the author's kit run, and by new bounded probes (a 99-return walk/jog matrix, the walk/jog-to-continuous boundary on two athletes, progression authority on two runners, a RETURN-mode control, an R6-H25 trace), each run on this freeze, on STATE-MODEL-CONSUMER-FREEZE-1 and on STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1.

claims.statement: Return steps are conditional on executed comparable work (R6-S21; R6 PP-7) and fitness declines with cessation (R6-S19): holding the entry dose for one complete week when the return's own week had only two of its sessions after the return is a bounded, conservative application of the approved conditional steps; the next step follows one executed week later and nothing earned is lost.
claims.applicability: Moderate (11-28 day) nonclinical returns reported mid-week.
limitations: Neither source sizes return steps; the step size (entry -> step 1 doubles easy minutes) is the policy's own.
counterevidence: Predefined progression was also effective in R6-S21; a one-week delay has negligible fitness cost either way.

claims.statement: Without the hold, step 1 would follow two short entry sessions (15 and 20 minutes) with easy runs doubling to 30 and the long run to 45 minutes.
claims.applicability: This probe and P05's control cell as the author describes it.
limitations: Synthetic timelines only; no real athlete, product data, human or empirical validation.
counterevidence: The single-run ceiling would still bound each run.

records.applicability: Mid-week moderate returns whose return week contains rows planned inside the declared pause.

decision.rationale: ACCEPT_WITH_REASON: a legitimate E7 + C3 (fail closed) consequence; not material under-dosing: one extra week at the entry dose, after a partial entry week, with history crediting what was executed.
preserve: E7 for the planner's review of a return's own week; C3 most-restrictive-first; C5 for HistoricalState.
decision.mec_change_level: None: a reading of approved rules.
decision.trade_off: One more entry week in exchange for a complete executed entry week before the dose doubles.
must_not: Must not hold the entry dose for more than one additional week on this ground.
Must not drop the executed sessions from history.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of 137 systematic reviews of randomized trials in healthy adults (>=18 y), resistance training >=6 wk; most evidence from novice trainees.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control; strength enhanced by heavier loads, 2-3 sets, >=2 sessions/wk and exercise at session start; hypertrophy by >=10 sets/muscle/wk; training to failure and periodization not consistently influential; perceived-exertion scales can raise absolute load with strength gains; individualization encouraged for adherence.
sources.locator: Abstract; Results (strength, hypertrophy); Discussion subsections Progressive overload, Specificity/Individualization, Variation.
limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.
No per-session increment, establishment or return procedure is specified.
counterevidence: States progression is not always necessary for benefit, so planned progression is a choice, not a requirement.

sources.title: Progressive overload without progressing load? The effects of load or repetition progression on muscular adaptations
sources.authors: Plotkin D, Coleman M, Van Every D, Maldonado J, Oberlin D, Israetel M, Feather J, Alto A, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 43 resistance-trained adults (>=1 y), 8 wk, 4 sets of 4 lower-body exercises 2x/wk; load progression versus repetition progression.
sources.findings: Both progressions produced similar hypertrophy, strength and endurance; small differences of questionable practical significance.
limitations: Trained participants; 8 weeks; lower body only.
counterevidence: Strength slightly favoured load progression.

counterevidence: The predecessor's extra week is also defensible; neither is wrong.

claims.statement: The regain caps hold one week longer, which is the conservative side of D56 (a cap rises only after a whole week).
claims.applicability: Reduced return weeks (systemic fatigue, unavailable day, equipment window).
limitations: Synthetic timelines only; no real athlete, product data, human or empirical validation.
counterevidence: One more capped week for those athletes.

records.applicability: Short returns after a week inside a return; strength rows.

decision.rationale: The divergence is approved by design (E7 for the planner, C5 for history) and produces coherent prescriptions: no dose above the executed one, the release earned by a full executed week, caps and ceilings respected (more conservative on regain caps).
preserve: E7 and C5 as approved; D56; the return ceiling (the last executed dose).

decision.trade_off: One week earlier load release (earned) and one week longer regain caps (conservative).
must_not: Must not release a load before a full executed week at the prior load after the return.

sources.title: Individualized Endurance Training Based on Recovery and Training Status in Recreational Runners
sources.authors: Nuuttila OP, Nummela A, Korhonen E, Hakkinen K, Kyrolainen H
sources.population_design_dose: 30 recreational runners, matched-pair randomized, 15 wk; predefined program (2 progressive weeks with +10% volume then a -25% recovery week) versus load adjusted twice weekly from HRV, perceived recovery and HR-speed index.
sources.findings: Both groups improved; individualized group improved 10-km time more (-6.2% versus -2.9%) with fewer low responders; HIT block used 6x3 min at maximal sustainable effort.
limitations: Small sample; HRV-dependent monitoring; negligible strength training.
counterevidence: Predefined progression was also effective.

literature_snapshot.counterevidence_search: Counterevidence was sought by re-running my unchanged kit and R7ASC probes on the frozen runtime with predecessor controls, by reproducing the author's kit run, and by new bounded probes (a 99-return walk/jog matrix, the walk/jog-to-continuous boundary on two athletes, progression authority on two runners, a RETURN-mode control, an R6-H25 trace), each run on this freeze, on STATE-MODEL-CONSUMER-FREEZE-1 and on STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1.
